intro: The Daintree is the lowland rainforest of tropical north Queensland, between the Daintree River and Cape Tribulation, where the forest runs down to the sea. At the Daintree Discovery Centre at Cow Bay, a boardwalk passes a strangler fig whose fused roots climb into the canopy around the space where its host tree once stood. A reader sent us its photograph and puts it at 500 to 600 years old.

question_answer: The Strangler Fig of the Daintree Discovery Centre stands on the centre's rainforest boardwalk at Cow Bay. A reader puts it at 500 to 600 years old; we have no measurement of our own.
question_context: A reader sent us this strangler fig from the rainforest boardwalk of the Daintree Discovery Centre at Cow Bay, north of the Daintree River in tropical north Queensland. They put it at 500 to 600 years old; that figure is theirs, not a measurement we have seen. Their photograph looks straight up a column of fused, latticed roots that leans out and climbs into the canopy among fan palms, with a visitor at the rail below for scale. A strangler fig begins as a seed dropped high in another tree, sends its roots down to the soil and slowly encloses its host, which dies and rots away; as the reader put it, the original tree it began its life on is gone. Because the fig's trunk is a net of roots around an empty core, it keeps no rings to count, so ages like this one are estimates. The centre charges for entry and its boardwalks are open in daytime.

trees.story:
A reader sent us this strangler fig from the boardwalks of the Daintree Discovery Centre at Cow Bay, in the lowland rainforest north of the Daintree River. "The original tree it began its life on is gone," they wrote, and that one line is the whole life story of a strangler.

A strangler fig starts as a seed left by a bird or a bat high in the crown of another tree. Its roots come down the host's trunk to the soil, thicken, and fuse into a net, until the host inside dies and rots away. What is left is a fig standing on its own roots around an empty space.

The photograph looks straight up the result. A column of roots, twisted and laced together, leans out from the left and climbs into the canopy, fan palms spreading their fronds around it and a visitor at the boardwalk rail looking small below.

The reader puts it at 500 to 600 years old. That is their figure; we have not seen a measurement or a count, and a hollow fig keeps no rings to count. If the centre's own guides give it an age, tell us here.

Look up through the trunk where the host once stood.
